Maxwell's electromagnetic theory treats light as a **continuous wave**, and that is
exactly what the **photoelectric effect** contradicts.
**Step 1 — recall what the theory did explain.**
**interference** ✓ **diffraction** ✓ **polarisation** ✓
All three are wave phenomena, and the electromagnetic theory handles them completely -
polarisation in particular, since it identifies light as a **transverse** wave of
electric and magnetic fields.
**Step 2 — recall what it could not explain.** The **photoelectric effect** ✓
**The three fatal observations.**
**threshold frequency**: below a certain ν, **no** electrons are emitted however intense
the light ✓ On a wave theory, a dim beam should simply take longer to accumulate the
needed energy.
**instantaneous emission**: electrons appear within **10⁻⁹ s** ✓ A wave would need hours
to deliver enough energy to a single atom at low intensity.
**energy independent of intensity**: the maximum kinetic energy depends on **frequency**
alone ✓ Intensity changes only the **number** of electrons, not their speed - the exact
opposite of what a wave predicts.
**Einstein's resolution, 1905.** Light is absorbed in **quanta** of energy hν:
K_max = **hν − φ** ✓
The threshold is where hν = φ; emission is instantaneous because one photon is absorbed
whole; and intensity means **more photons**, not more energetic ones.
**A worked instance.** Sodium, φ = 2·3 eV. Green light at 550 nm gives hν = **2·25 eV**
✓ just below threshold - **no** emission, however bright. Blue at 450 nm gives
**2·76 eV**, and electrons emerge with up to **0·46 eV** ✓
**Why this did not overthrow the wave theory.** Interference and diffraction remain
inexplicable on a pure particle picture ✓ Both are needed: **wave-particle duality**,
with the wave description governing propagation and the photon description emission and
absorption.
**The other quantum failures of classical theory.** **Black-body radiation** (the
ultraviolet catastrophe), the **Compton effect** and **atomic spectra** ✓ all demanding
the same quantisation.
**Why Einstein received the Nobel Prize for this.** Not for relativity, but for the
photoelectric law ✓ - the 1921 prize, awarded once Millikan's painstaking measurements
had confirmed the straight line of K_max against ν and yielded **h** directly.
∴ Photo electric effect.

Coherent sources add **amplitudes**; incoherent sources add **intensities**.
**Step 1 — find the coherent intensity.** At the central maximum the two waves are in
phase, so the amplitudes add:
A_total = A + A = **2A** ✓
I₀ ∝ (2A)² = **4A²** ✓
**Step 2 — find the incoherent intensity.** With no fixed phase relation the
interference term averages to **zero**, and the intensities simply add:
I ∝ A² + A² = **2A²** ✓
**Step 3 — form the ratio.**
I/I₀ = 2A²/4A² = ½
I = **I₀/2** ✓
**The general superposition formula.**
I = I₁ + I₂ + **2√(I₁I₂) cos δ** ✓
The last term is the **interference** term. For coherent sources in phase, cos δ = 1 and
it contributes fully; for incoherent sources ⟨cos δ⟩ = **0** and it vanishes.
**Why incoherent light shows no fringes.** The phase difference δ **fluctuates
randomly** and far faster than the eye or any detector can follow ✓ so what is observed
is the time average - uniform illumination of intensity 2A² everywhere.
**Why energy is still conserved with coherent sources.** The central maximum has
**twice** the incoherent intensity, but the dark fringes have **zero** ✓ Averaged over
the screen, interference **redistributes** energy rather than creating it: the mean of
4A² and 0 is 2A², exactly the incoherent value.
**What coherence requires.** A **constant** phase difference over the observation time ✓
Two independent lamps can never provide it, because each atom radiates for only about
**10⁻⁸ s** before its phase jumps at random.
**How coherence is achieved in practice.** By **division of wavefront** (Young's slits,
the biprism) or **division of amplitude** (thin films, the Michelson interferometer) ✓
In every case one source is split, so the two beams share the same phase history.
**Why a laser is different.** **Stimulated** emission makes all the photons share one
phase ✓ which is why two separate lasers can, with care, be made to interfere.
**Reading the distractors.** **I₀** ✗ would mean coherence makes no difference. **2I₀** ✗
and **4I₀** ✗ would make the incoherent case the **brighter**, which inverts the
physics ✓ Incoherent light must give **less** at the maximum.
∴ I₀/2.

An unpolarised beam has its vibrations distributed **uniformly over all directions**, so
a polaroid transmits exactly **half**.
**Step 1 — describe unpolarised light.** Its electric vector takes **every** orientation
perpendicular to the ray, with equal probability and in rapid random succession ✓
**Step 2 — resolve along the pass axis.** A vibration at angle θ contributes
I₀cos²θ ✓
**Step 3 — average over all angles.**
⟨cos²θ⟩ = **½** ✓ over a full rotation.
**Step 4 — conclude.**
I = **I₀/2** ✓
**Why the average of cos²θ is one half.** Because ⟨cos²θ⟩ + ⟨sin²θ⟩ = 1 and, by
symmetry, the two averages are equal ✓ This is the same reason the r.m.s. value of a
sine wave is 1/√2 of its peak.
**The contrast with Malus's law.** For light **already polarised**,
I = I₀cos²θ ✓
depending on the angle. For **unpolarised** light the answer is I₀/2 **whatever** the
orientation of the polaroid - which is why rotating a single polaroid in a beam of
ordinary light produces **no change** in brightness.
**That test in the laboratory.** Rotate one polaroid: if the brightness is constant, the
light is **unpolarised**; if it varies but never vanishes, **partially** polarised; if
it falls to **zero** twice per turn, **plane** polarised ✓
**Two polaroids in series.**
first: I₀/2 ✓
second, at θ to the first: **(I₀/2)cos²θ** ✓
**crossed** (θ = 90°): **zero** ✓
**The surprising three-polaroid result.** Insert a third at 45° between two crossed
ones, and light **reappears**:
(I₀/2)cos²45° x cos²45° = **I₀/8** ✓ a vivid demonstration that a polaroid does not
merely filter but **projects** the vibration onto a new direction.
**Why the real figure is below 50%.** An actual sheet absorbs and reflects a little even
along its pass axis ✓ Good polaroid transmits about **40%** of unpolarised light rather
than the ideal 50%.
**Where this matters.** Polaroid sunglasses dim everything by half, but cut **glare**
far more, because light reflected from water or road is already largely polarised
horizontally and the lens's axis is **vertical** ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **I₀** ✗ would mean the polaroid does nothing. **I₀/4** ✗
is the result after a **second** polaroid at 45°. **Zero** ✗ would require the incoming
light to be polarised across the axis ✓
∴ I₀/2.

The sea looks blue for the same reason the sky does - **scattering**.
**Step 1 — identify the mechanism.** Sunlight entering the water is **scattered** by the
water molecules themselves ✓
**Step 2 — recall the wavelength dependence.** Rayleigh scattering goes as
I ∝ **1/λ⁴** ✓
so **blue** (450 nm) is scattered roughly **(700/450)⁴ ≈ 6** times as strongly as red ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** The scattered light reaching the eye is predominantly **blue** ✓
**The second mechanism, equally important.** Water **absorbs** red and infrared strongly
✓ At 10 m depth, about **85%** of the red light has gone, while blue penetrates to
**100 m** and beyond. So the deep sea is blue both because blue is scattered back and
because red is removed.
**Why this is not simply the sky's reflection.** The sea is blue even when the sky is
**overcast** ✓ and it looks blue when viewed from below the surface by a diver, where no
sky is visible. Reflection contributes, but it is not the cause.
**Why the 1/λ⁴ law holds.** When the scatterers are much **smaller** than the
wavelength, the induced dipole radiates as ω⁴ ✓ Lord Rayleigh derived this in 1871, and
it explains the blue sky, the red sunset and the blue of deep water alike.
**Why sunsets are red.** At low elevation the light traverses a long path, and the blue
is scattered **out** of the direct beam, leaving the red to reach the eye ✓ The same
physics, viewed from the other end.
**Why coastal water looks green or brown.** Suspended sediment and **phytoplankton**
scatter and absorb differently ✓ Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red, reflecting green -
which is why productive waters appear green and satellite ocean-colour sensors can map
plankton from orbit.
**C. V. Raman's part in this.** Dissatisfied with Rayleigh's claim that the sea merely
reflects the sky, Raman investigated molecular scattering in liquids ✓ The work led him
to the **Raman effect** and the 1930 Nobel Prize - a line of enquiry begun on a voyage
home across the Mediterranean.
**Reading the distractors.** **Interference** of reflected light ✗ gives the colours of
thin films, not of a deep body of water. The **image of the sky** ✗ fails for overcast
days and for the view from underwater ✓
∴ scattering of sunlight by the water molecules.

Matter waves were confirmed by **diffraction** - the phenomenon no particle picture can
produce.
**Step 1 — recall de Broglie's hypothesis, 1924.**
λ = **h/p** ✓ Every particle has a wavelength.
**Step 2 — recall how to test it.** Diffract the particles from a grating whose spacing
matches λ ✓ For electrons at a few tens of volts, λ is about **1 Å** - the spacing of
atoms in a **crystal**, which therefore serves as the grating.
**Step 3 — recall G. P. Thomson's experiment, 1927.** He passed a beam of fast electrons
through a **thin gold foil** and photographed the transmitted beam ✓ It produced
concentric **diffraction rings**, exactly like the Debye-Scherrer rings X-rays give from
a polycrystalline sample.
**Step 4 — read the conclusion.** Rings can only arise from **waves** ✓ and measuring
their radii gave λ in precise agreement with h/p.
**The companion experiment.** **Davisson and Germer**, the same year, reflected
electrons from a **nickel** crystal and found a sharp maximum at 50° for 54 eV
electrons ✓ satisfying the Bragg condition with λ = **1·67 Å**, against the predicted
h/p = 1·67 Å.
**The calculation for 54 eV electrons.**
λ = h/√(2mеV) = **12·27/√V Å** ✓
= 12·27/√54 = **1·67 Å** ✓
**The famous irony.** **J. J. Thomson** won the Nobel Prize for showing the electron is
a **particle**; his son **G. P. Thomson** won it for showing the electron is a **wave** ✓
Both were right - the 1937 prize went to G. P. Thomson with Davisson.
**Why the other phenomena will not do.**
**refraction** ✗ bending at a boundary, explicable by particles too - Newton used it
**scattering** ✗ a collision effect, thoroughly particle-like
**polarisation** ✗ needs a **transverse** wave, and matter waves are not transverse ✓
Only **diffraction** - the spreading and interference of a wave at an obstacle - is
decisive.
**The modern descendants.** **Electron microscopy** exploits the short de Broglie
wavelength for resolution far beyond light; **neutron diffraction** locates hydrogen
atoms that X-rays cannot see ✓ Matter-wave diffraction has become a working tool, not
merely a proof.
**How far it extends.** Diffraction has been demonstrated with atoms, with buckyballs of
60 carbon atoms, and with molecules of 2000 atoms ✓ The hypothesis holds for everything;
for macroscopic bodies λ is simply too small to detect.
∴ diffraction.

A glass plate in one path **shifts** the pattern but leaves the fringe **width**
unchanged.
**Step 1 — write the fringe width.**
β = **λD/d** ✓
It depends only on the wavelength, the screen distance and the slit separation.
**Step 2 — see what the plate changes.** It introduces an extra **optical path** in one
arm:
Δ = **(µ − 1)t** ✓ a **constant**, the same for every point on the screen.
**Step 3 — see the consequence.** A constant added path shifts the **whole** pattern
sideways, but the **spacing** between consecutive fringes is untouched ✓
β = **0·3 mm**, as before ✓
**Why the spacing cannot change.** The fringe separation depends on how fast the path
difference **varies across the screen**, which is governed by d and D ✓ The plate adds
the same amount everywhere, so the rate of change is unaltered.
**How far the pattern shifts.**
y₀ = **(µ − 1)tD/d** = (µ − 1)tβ/λ ✓
With µ = 1·5 the shift is 0·5t D/d - towards the side carrying the plate, since the
light there is retarded and the zero-order fringe must move to compensate.
**A worked instance.** With t = 10 µm, λ = 600 nm and β = 0·3 mm:
number of fringes shifted = (µ − 1)t/λ = 0·5(10 x 10⁻⁶)/(600 x 10⁻⁹) = **8·3 fringes** ✓
a shift of 2·5 mm - large and easily measured.
**Why this is a useful technique.** Measuring the shift gives **µ** or **t** with great
precision ✓ It is the principle of the Rayleigh interferometer and of refractometry in
general; a shift of a tenth of a fringe is detectable.
**Where the central white fringe goes.** With white light, the fringe of **zero path
difference** - the white one - moves to the side with the plate ✓ which is how the shift
is identified unambiguously among otherwise similar fringes.
**What would change the fringe width.** Altering **λ**, **d** or **D** ✓ or immersing the
whole apparatus in a liquid, which shortens λ to λ/µ and so **narrows** the fringes.
**Why "zero" is wrong.** The fringes do not disappear ✓ Both beams still arrive, still
coherent; only their relative phase is offset.
**Reading the distractors.** **0·45 mm** ✗ multiplies by µ = 1·5; **0·15 mm** ✗ divides
by it ✓ Both suppose the plate alters the geometry, which it does not.
∴ 0.3 mm.

Newton's corpuscles were **attracted** into the denser medium, so they travelled
**faster** there - and therefore **slower in the rarer** medium.
**Step 1 — recall the model.** Light is a stream of tiny **particles** emitted by the
source ✓
**Step 2 — explain refraction on it.** At the boundary the denser medium attracts the
corpuscles **normally** ✓ so the component of velocity **perpendicular** to the surface
increases while the parallel component is unchanged. The ray bends **towards** the
normal - which is what is observed.
**Step 3 — read off the speeds.**
v_denser = **greater** ✓
v_rarer = **lesser** ✓
**Step 4 — write the refractive index it predicts.**
µ = **v_denser/v_rarer** ✓ greater than 1, as required.
**The wave theory's opposite prediction.** Huygens' construction gives
µ = **v_rarer/v_denser** ✓ so light must travel **slower** in the denser medium. Here
the two theories part company irreconcilably.
**The decisive experiment.** **Foucault**, 1850, using a rotating mirror, measured the
speed of light in **water** and found it about **three quarters** of the value in air ✓
The wave theory was right; Newton's corpuscular theory was wrong.
**The modern value.** c/n = 3 x 10⁸/1·33 = **2·25 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹** in water ✓ exactly as
Foucault found.
**Why it took 170 years to settle.** The experiment demands measuring a difference in
the speed of light over a path of a few metres ✓ Only Foucault's and Fizeau's rotating
mirrors and toothed wheels made that possible.
**What the corpuscular theory did explain.** **Rectilinear propagation** and sharp
shadows - naturally, since particles travel in straight lines ✓ and **reflection**, as
elastic bouncing. These successes, and Newton's authority, kept it dominant for a
century.
**What it never explained.** **Interference**, **diffraction** and **polarisation** ✓
Young's double-slit experiment of 1801 made the first of these inescapable.
**The curious epilogue.** The **photon** restored a particle aspect to light in 1905 ✓
but the photon is nothing like a Newtonian corpuscle: it carries no mass, always travels
at c in vacuum, and its propagation is governed by a wave.
**Reading the distractors.** **Lesser in denser medium** ✗ is the **wave** theory's
prediction - and the true one, but not what the question asks. **Independent of the
medium** ✗ and **same in all media** ✗ say the same thing, and neither theory claims it ✓
∴ lesser in rarer medium.

All three statements are correct: the slit S is needed only when the source is both
extended and spatially incoherent.
**Step 1 — examine (a).** An **ordinary extended source** ✓ Different points of it are
mutually incoherent and each produces its own fringe pattern, displaced from the others.
The patterns overlap and **wash out**. A narrow slit S selects a small region, making the
illumination of the two slits spatially coherent. **Necessary** ✓
**Step 2 — examine (b).** A **well collimated** beam ✓ Collimation means the light
arrives as plane wavefronts, so a single wavefront reaches both slits and their phase
relation is fixed. S is then **not needed** ✓
**Step 3 — examine (c).** A **spatially coherent** source ✓ This is by definition a
source whose field has a fixed phase relation across the width spanning both slits - a
laser, for instance. S would serve no purpose. **Not needed** ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** (a), (b) and (c) are **all** correct ✓
**What the slit S actually does.** It enforces **spatial coherence** by restricting the
source to a width small enough that the two slits sample one coherent patch ✓ The price
is a great loss of light, which is why Young's experiment is dim with a lamp and
brilliant with a laser.
**The coherence-width condition.**
a_source x d/D < **λ** roughly ✓ where a_source is the source width. Exceed it and the
fringes lose contrast; the formal statement is the **van Cittert-Zernike** theorem.
**A worked instance.** With a lamp 1 mm wide, slits 1 mm apart and the source 1 m away:
(10⁻³)(10⁻³)/1 = **10⁻⁶ m** ✓ far larger than λ = 6 x 10⁻⁷ m, so the fringes are badly
blurred. Narrowing S to 0·1 mm restores them.
**Why temporal coherence is a separate matter.** That concerns the **spectral width** -
how monochromatic the light is - and limits the **number** of visible fringes, not their
formation ✓ White light gives only a handful of coloured fringes near the centre for
this reason.
**Why a laser needs neither S nor a monochromator.** It is both spatially and temporally
coherent to a high degree ✓ which is why the modern demonstration simply shines a laser
pointer at a double slit and projects metres-wide fringes.
**What collimation does not guarantee.** A collimated beam from an **extended** source
can still be spatially incoherent if it has angular spread ✓ "Well collimated" in
statement (b) is doing real work: it implies the angular spread is small enough.
**Reading the distractors.** Each omits one true statement ✓ Testing the three
independently - does this source illuminate both slits coherently? - settles it.
∴ a), b) and c).
